entry: Any of six chemical elements in group 2 of the periodic table. They are [[Beryllium|beryllium]] (Be), [[Magnesium|magnesium]] (Mg), [[Calcium|calcium]] (Ca), [[Strontium|strontium]] (Sr), [[Barium|barium]] (Ba) and [[Radium|radium]] (Ra). All are shiny, silvery-white, somewhat reactive metals, and all are less reactive than the [[Alkali metal|alkali metals]] at standard temperature and pressure. Each has two electrons in its outer s orbital, which they readily lose to form ions with a +2 charge. Beryllium's chloride, bromide and iodide are covalent, while the halides of the other members are ionic crystalline compounds. All members except beryllium react with water to form strongly alkaline hydroxides, and the heavier ones react more vigorously. Radium occurs in nature only through the decay of uranium and thorium, and its chemistry is not well established because of its radioactivity. Calcium and magnesium are among the most abundant elements in the Earth's crust.

Broad class of naturally occurring organic compounds containing at least one nitrogen atom. Alkaloids are produced by bacteria, fungi, plants and animals. Many have pharmacological effects: quinine is antimalarial, ephedrine has antiasthma activity, and [[Morphine]] is an [[Analgesic|analgesic]]. Stimulant alkaloids include [[Caffeine]], [[Nicotine]] and [[Cocaine]], while atropine and tubocurarine are toxic. Most alkaloids are basic, though some are neutral or weakly acidic. [[Amine|Amines]], amino acid peptides, proteins and nucleic acids are usually not classed as alkaloids. The name was introduced in 1819 by German chemist Carl Friedrich Wilhelm Meissner. Alkaloid-containing plants have been used since ancient times; medicinal plants were known in [[Mesopotamia]] from about 2000 BC. Morphine, isolated from the [[Opium|opium]] poppy in 1805 by Friedrich Sertürner, is considered the first recognized plant alkaloid.

Acyclic saturated [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbon]] in which all carbon–carbon bonds are single. Alkanes, also called paraffins, have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and range from [[Methane|methane]] (CH₄) to very large molecules such as hexacontane (C₆₀H₁₂₂). Their carbon atoms form a tree-like structure, and the number of carbon atoms gives the molecule's size. Alkanes with more than about 17 carbon atoms are waxes, solid at standard ambient temperature and pressure. Successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit, forming a homologous series. IUPAC restricts the name to acyclic compounds, though some sources include cycloalkanes. Methane is produced by [[Archaea|methanogenic archaea]], and some long-chain alkanes act as [[Pheromone|pheromones]] or protective plant waxes. The two main commercial sources are [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and [[Natural gas]]. Butane has two isomers, [[Butane|n-butane]] and isobutane, and the number of isomers rises rapidly with size.

Unsaturated [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbon]] with one or more carbon–carbon double bonds. Alkenes, also called olefins, form a series with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, two hydrogens fewer than the corresponding [[Alkane|alkane]]. A double bond consists of a sigma bond and a pi bond. It is stronger than a single bond (611 kJ/mol against 347 kJ/mol) and shorter (1.33 Å against 1.53 Å). Rotation about the double bond is restricted, so cis and trans isomers can be handled separately. Alkenes are generally colorless, nonpolar and more reactive than alkanes. They are produced industrially by steam cracking and dehydrogenation of hydrocarbons from natural-gas condensate and [[Petroleum|petroleum]]. The simplest, [[Ethylene|ethylene]] (C₂H₄), is the organic compound produced on the largest scale, at approximately 225 million metric tons per year as of 2024. Ethylene and [[Propylene|propylene]] are the feedstocks for [[Polyethylene]] and [[Polypropylene]].

Unsaturated [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbon]] containing at least one carbon–carbon triple bond. Alkynes are traditionally known as [[Acetylene|acetylenes]], although that name refers specifically to C₂H₂, called ethyne. The simplest acyclic alkynes with one triple bond form a series with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. In acetylene the H–C≡C bond angles are 180°, making alkynes rod-like, and cyclic alkynes are rare because of bond strain. The C≡C bond, 118 pm long, is shorter than the C=C bond of an [[Alkene|alkene]] (132 pm) and the C–C bond of an [[Alkane|alkane]] (153 pm). The triple bond is very strong, at 839 kJ/mol. Terminal alkynes (RC≡CH) are mildly acidic, with pKa values of around 25, far more acidic than alkenes and alkanes. Alkynes with four or more carbon atoms form structural isomers according to the position of the triple bond.

headword: All Quiet on the Western Front
sort_key: all quiet on the western front
entry: Semi-autobiographical novel by Erich Maria Remarque, a German veteran of [[World War I]]. Serialized in 1928 and published in book form in January 1929, it depicts the physical and mental trauma of German soldiers on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] and their detachment from civilian life after returning home. The book sold 2.5 million copies in 22 languages in its first 18 months in print. It was among the books banned and burned in [[Nazi Germany]]. The 1930 American film adaptation, directed by Lewis Milestone, won two [[Academy Awards]].

[[Arabic]] term for God. Principally associated with [[Islam]], where it is also the proper name of God, the word is thought to derive by contraction from *al-ilāh* ('the god') and is related to other [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] names for God, such as Aramaic *ʼElāhā* and Hebrew *ʾĔlōah*. In pre-Islamic Arabia, Allah was the supreme deity, worshipped alongside lesser deities. Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians have also used the term for God. Whether Allah can be considered a personal name of God is disputed among scholars.

Allegory in Book VII of [[Plato]]'s *Republic*. Plato presents it to compare the effect of [[Education|education]] and its lack on human nature. Prisoners chained since childhood face a cave wall and see only shadows cast by objects carried past a fire behind them; they take the echoing voices of the carriers to belong to the shadows. A prisoner freed from the cave comes to understand the true source of the images, and eventually the sunlit world outside. [[Socrates]] narrates the allegory in a dialogue with Glaucon.

American former professional basketball player. Nicknamed 'the Answer', he played 14 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA), mainly for the [[Philadelphia]] 76ers. He was the NBA Rookie of the Year in 1996–97 and Most Valuable Player in 2000–01, when he led the 76ers to the NBA Finals. A four-time scoring champion and 11-time All-Star, he was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2016. His playoff scoring average of 29.7 points per game trails only [[Michael Jordan]] and Luka Dončić.

Military coalition that opposed the [[Axis powers]] from 1939 to 1945. Its principal members were the 'Big Four': the [[United Kingdom]], the [[Soviet Union]], the [[United States]] and the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]]. Formally called the [[United Nations]] from 1942, when 26 countries signed the Declaration by United Nations, the coalition was joined by many more countries. The Soviet Union joined after the German invasion in June 1941, and the United States after the Japanese attack on [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|Pearl Harbor]] in December 1941. The Allies became the basis of the United Nations after the war.

Military coalition, also called the Entente, that opposed the [[Central Powers]] (Germany, [[Austria-Hungary]], the [[Ottoman Empire]] and Bulgaria) in 1914–18. Led by France, the United Kingdom, the [[Russian Empire]], the [[United States]], the [[Kingdom of Italy]] and the [[Empire of Japan]], its core was the Triple Entente of 1907. Japan joined in 1914, Italy in 1915 and the United States in 1917 as an 'associated power'.

Large reptile in the genus *Alligator*, order Crocodilia. Two species survive: the American alligator (*A. mississippiensis*) and the Chinese alligator (*A. sinensis*). Alligators first appeared in the late [[Eocene]] about 37 million years ago. Alligators are native only to the United States and China. The American alligator ranges across the southeastern United States, with the largest populations in [[Florida]] and [[Louisiana]], each with over a million animals. Adult American alligators average 360 kg (790 lb) and 4 m (13 ft), and the largest recorded, found in Louisiana, measured 5.84 m (19.2 ft). The Chinese alligator is smaller, rarely exceeding 2.1 m (7 ft). Alligators commonly live up to 50 years. Southern Florida is the only place where alligators and [[Crocodile|crocodiles]] coexist.

Large species of freshwater turtle, the largest in North America. Its name refers to its powerful jaws and to the shell ridges that resemble [[Alligator|alligator]] skin; it is also called the loggerhead snapper. It is endemic to freshwater habitats of the [[United States]], from the Florida Panhandle west to East Texas. It is often associated with the [[Common snapping turtle]], which is not closely related. Three rows of spikes on the carapace flatten with age. A specimen at the Shedd Aquarium in [[Chicago]] weighed 113 kg (249 lb). Populations have declined through commercial harvesting and habitat degradation, and the species is classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN.

American actress. She played C. J. Cregg on the [[NBC]] series [[The West Wing]] (1999–2006), for which she won four Primetime Emmy Awards. In total she has won eight Primetime Emmys, including two for the [[CBS]] sitcom Mom. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as LaVona Golden in *I, Tonya* (2017). She has also been nominated for two Tony Awards for stage work.

Genus of large theropod dinosaur from the late [[Jurassic]] period. It lived about 156 to 143 million years ago. Othniel C. Marsh named it in 1877, meaning 'different lizard', for lightweight vertebrae he believed were unique. The genus includes at least three valid species, the best known being *A. fragilis*. Most remains come from the Morrison Formation of North America, and for over half of the 20th century the genus was known as *Antrodemus*. A large bipedal predator, *A. fragilis* averaged 7.5–8 m (25–26 ft) in length, with the largest estimated at 9 m (30 ft). As the most abundant large predator of the Morrison Formation, it probably preyed on large herbivores such as sauropods. Whether it hunted in packs or alone is debated.

Property of some [[Chemical element|chemical elements]] to exist in two or more forms in the same physical state. Each form, called an allotrope, differs in how its atoms are bonded or arranged. The term, from Greek *allos* ('other') and *tropos* ('manner'), was first proposed in 1840 by Jöns Jakob Berzelius. [[Carbon]] has allotropes including [[Diamond]], with a cubic lattice; [[Graphite]], with hexagonal sheets; [[Graphene]], a single sheet of graphite; and fullerenes. Oxygen has two allotropes, dioxygen and [[Ozone]]; ozone is a much stronger oxidizing agent. [[Iron]] changes from a body-centered cubic to a face-centered cubic structure above 906 °C. [[Phosphorus]] has numerous solid allotropes, all reverting to the same P₄ form when melted. The general term for compounds is polymorphism.

Dried unripe berry of the tree *Pimenta dioica*. The tree is native to the [[Greater Antilles]], southern Mexico and Central America, and is now cultivated in many warm regions. The English coined the name in 1621 because it combined the flavors of [[Cinnamon]], [[Nutmeg]] and [[Clove]], though it is not a mixture of spices. It is an important ingredient of West Indian cuisine and is used in Jamaican jerk seasoning. Jamaica remains the leading source of the plant.

Fan-shaped accumulation of sediment spreading outward from a concentrated source. Fans form where a flow of water, sediment or debris emerges from a confined channel, such as a narrow canyon, onto a flat plain; the reduced flow drops its load. They are most common at the foot of [[Desert|desert]] mountains and characteristic of arid to semiarid climates, though they also form in humid areas with intense rainfall and in glaciated regions. They range from less than 1 sq km (0.4 sq mi) to almost 20,000 sq km (7,700 sq mi), with slopes of 1.5 to 25 degrees. Some of the largest lie along the Himalaya front on the [[Indo-Gangetic Plain]], where a shift of the feeder channel can cause catastrophic flooding, as on the Kosi River fan in 2008. Fans are also found on [[Mars]] and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]].

Largest city in [[Kazakhstan]], in the foothills of the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains. With more than two million residents, it is the second-largest city in [[Central Asia]] after [[Tashkent]]. It was the capital of Kazakhstan from 1929 to 1991 and again until 1997, when the capital moved to Akmola, later renamed [[Astana]]. Formerly Alma-Ata, the city was renamed Almaty in 1993. It hosted the 1978 Alma-Ata Primary Healthcare Conference and the 2011 Asian Winter Games, and it was a contender for the 2022 Winter Olympics, which went to [[Beijing]]. It has been a UNESCO Creative City of Music since 2017. A disputed theory derives the name from the Kazakh word for 'apple'.

Species of tree in the genus *Prunus*, cultivated for its seed. The fruit is a drupe rather than a true [[Nut (fruit)|nut]]: a leathery hull surrounds a woody shell, which encloses the seed. Almonds were among the earliest domesticated fruit trees, because they could be grown reliably from seed. Domesticated almonds from the [[Bronze Age|Early Bronze Age]] have been found in the Middle East. The tree prospers in a [[Mediterranean climate]] with warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters. Trees bear an economic crop in the third year after planting and reach full bearing in five to six years. [[California]] produces about 80% of the world's supply, but water demand, pesticide use and drought raise concerns about sustainability. Almonds feature in many cuisines, notably in desserts such as marzipan.

[[Berbers|Berber]] Muslim dynasty centered in present-day [[Morocco]] (1050s–1147). It emerged from a coalition of nomadic Berber tribes in what is now [[Mauritania]] and Western Sahara, led by the religious reformer Abdallah ibn Yasin, who sought to impose strict [[Sunni Islam]]. The name derives from the Arabic *al-Murābiṭūn*, 'those from the *ribats*', or fortified monasteries. The dynasty founded [[Marrakesh]] as a capital around 1070 and extended control over the western [[Maghreb]] and [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]]. Its victory at Sagrajas in 1086 temporarily halted Christian advances in Iberia. Almoravid power in al-Andalus declined after the loss of [[Zaragoza]] in 1118, and the Almohads captured Marrakesh in 1147.

Genus of flowering succulent plants. Most species have a rosette of large, fleshy leaves, and their tubular flowers are often yellow, orange, pink or red. The genus is native to tropical and southern Africa, [[Madagascar]], the [[Arabian Peninsula]], India and Indian Ocean islands. The APG IV system (2016) places it in the family Asphodelaceae; earlier it was assigned to [[Liliaceae]]. Molecular studies from 2010 onward suggested that the genus should be divided, and in 2014 it was split into six genera. *Aloe vera*, the best-known species, is cultivated for topical uses and dietary supplements and is used in folk and [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]]. Many species are grown as ornamentals.

headword: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
sort_key: along the river during the qingming festival
entry: Handscroll painting generally attributed to Zhang Zeduan of the [[Song dynasty]]. It depicts daily life and the landscape of the capital, Bianjing (present-day Kaifeng), during the Northern Song. Read from right to left, the scroll reveals all levels of society, from rich to poor, and the economic activity of both countryside and city. The original, 25.5 cm (10.0 in) high and 5.25 m (5.74 yd) long, contains 814 human figures, 28 boats and 60 animals. Hundreds of later copies exist, and the painting is often called 'China's [[Mona Lisa|Mona Lisa]]'. It was a favorite of [[Puyi]], the last emperor of China, who took it when he left the [[Forbidden City]] in 1924. It was recovered in 1945 and is kept at the Palace Museum, and it is exhibited only briefly because of its fragility.

[[Autoimmune disease|Autoimmune]] condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body. Also called spot baldness, it usually causes a few coin-sized bald patches on the scalp. It is believed to result from a breach in the immune privilege of [[Hair|hair]] follicles.About 2% of people are affected at some point, usually beginning in childhood, and females at higher rates than males. Hair regrows within a year in more than 50% of sudden-onset patchy cases, though many people have more than one episode. No cure is known, but triamcinolone injections and 5% minoxidil cream speed regrowth.

Domesticated species of South American camelid, bred mainly for its fiber. Alpacas were traditionally herded in the [[Andes]] of southern [[Peru]], western [[Bolivia]], [[Ecuador]] and northern [[Chile]]. A DNA study presented in 2001 showed that the alpaca descends from the [[Vicuña|vicuña]], its wild relative, rather than from the [[Llama|llama]]. Two breeds are recognized: the Suri, whose fiber grows in straight locks, and the Huacaya, whose crimped fiber grows in bundles. Alpacas are shorter than llamas and are bred mainly for [[Wool|wool]], while llamas were prized as pack animals and livestock guardians. Alpacas were domesticated at least 5,000 to 6,000 years ago. About 4 million alpacas were reported worldwide in 2024, roughly 87% of them in Peru.
